title: Cake: So Great. So, So Great
summary: Josh and Chuck explore cake: their personal favorites (Publix yellow sheet cake, red velvet with Waldorf frosting, carrot cake, Japanese cheesecake), the etymology of "cake," ancient and medieval origins, the American Industrial Revolution cake boom, the chemistry of baking (leavening agents, yeast, air incorporation, baking soda and baking powder, fats, sugar, eggs, flour and gluten, liquids and steam), oven tips and doneness tests, cooling in the pan, the history of cake mixes (P. Duff and Sons, Ernest Dichter myth), frosting history, red velvet cake color, regional cakes, and cooking methods. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about Nick Pagan's care package and a game of Stuff You Should Know trivia counts.

segments.title: Opening banter and favorite cakes
segments.summary: Hosts riff on candy and office snacks, then debate favorite cakes, including Publix yellow sheet cake with buttercream, red velvet, carrot cake, and Japanese cheesecake.

segments.title: Early cake history and etymology
segments.summary: The word cake is traced to Old Norse 'kaka', and medieval cakes were a sweeter version of bread. Cakes are said to date to ancient Egypt, with honey and grain cooked on hot stones. The Greeks made round cakes with candles for Artemis, and Germans later made birthday cakes. Many familiar cakes are actually 19th-century American developments from the Industrial Revolution.

segments.title: Leavening and the chemistry of cake
segments.summary: Hosts describe baking as chemistry. Leavening was once done with yeast and by beating eggs for long periods, until chemical leaveners arrived in the mid-19th century. Baking soda reacts with an acid to release CO2, which makes cakes rise. Air from creaming and sifting also contributes.

segments.title: Fats, sugar, eggs, flour and liquids
segments.summary: Fats such as butter, shortening, margarine and oil add moisture and texture; butter also traps air when creamed. Sugar binds water and tenderizes, and it helps with browning. Egg yolks provide structure and emulsifiers. Flour forms gluten with water, with cake flour having less protein than all-purpose or bread flour. Liquids create steam that expands air cells during baking.

segments.title: Ovens, doneness and cooling
segments.summary: The enclosed oven, spreading in the 18th century, gave consistent heat for home baking. Opening the oven door can cause cakes to fall. Hosts discuss oven windows and lights, the toothpick test, the spring-back tap test, and letting cakes cool in the pan before inverting onto a wire rack.

segments.title: Baking powder and cake mix history
segments.summary: Baking powder, which combines baking soda with dry acids, came about twenty years after baking soda and simplified cake making. P. Duff and Sons of Pittsburgh created a gingerbread mix from surplus molasses in the 1930s, which led to packaged cake mixes. The myth that cake mixes came from World War Two flour surplus is debunked, and the Ernest Dichter guilt-and-eggs focus group story is described as a myth, though Dichter is credited with promoting decorating and frosting.

segments.title: Frosting history and red velvet color
segments.summary: The earliest frostings were almond and sugar pastes. The first iced layer cake is credited to a fifteenth-century cook, and frosting recipes spread later. Hosts discuss fondant and buttercream, and say red velvet's color comes from a reaction of cocoa, vinegar and buttermilk, as reported by a source they read.

segments.title: Cooking methods and regional cakes
segments.summary: Creaming, non-aeration (flourless cheesecake, water bath, folding), foaming (meringue, Pavlova with Australia and New Zealand dispute), all-in-one methods are covered. Hosts discuss shortbread etymology, Emily's gluten-free shortcake, and regional and American-invented cakes such as hummingbird cake, Indian pudding cake, chocolate layer cake, German chocolate cake, pineapple upside-down cake, and Black Forest cake.

segments.title: Japanese and other international cakes
segments.summary: Hosts discuss Japanese cakes such as dorayaki, Japanese cheesecake, and tres leches. They touch on Japan's refinement of French baking.

segments.title: Listener mail: Nick Pagan and trivia counts
segments.summary: Hosts thank listener Nick Pagan for a care package that included a framed poster, CDs, wine, bourbon and Scotch, and a list of films and show topics. They play a game guessing counts of COAs, take-twos, listener mail shout-outs, Simpsons references, and high-fives, and read Josh's nicknames for Chuck. They close with calls to action for social media and the website.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Brief closing: the hosts say there is a cake out there for everyone and sign off with the show's web and social links.
